title: ResDIF: A Residual Disentanglement Framework for Interpretable Financial Time Series Forecasting via Spectrally-Enhanced Temporal Encoding

problem.claim: Stock trend prediction and market attribution are challenged by low signal-to-noise ratios and non-stationarity caused by coupled market, sector, and idiosyncratic dynamics.

gap.claim: Existing methods struggle to capture dynamic multi-scale dependencies and lack the interpretability needed for return attribution.

contributions.claim: ResDIF uses a progressive residual architecture with spectrally enhanced temporal encoding to decompose stock data into market, sector, and individual layers.
A self-supervised orthogonal loss encourages feature separation and decouples systematic risks from idiosyncratic alpha.
The framework uses structural interpretability to support adaptive portfolio optimization through dynamic hedging and asset selection.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that ResDIF unifies high predictive accuracy with granular structural attribution.
Experiments reportedly show that ResDIF outperforms existing methods and provides actionable interpretability support for portfolio risk management.

narrative_sequence.summary: Financial forecasting and market attribution are important for investment and risk control.
Coupled hierarchical drivers create low signal-to-noise ratios and non-stationarity.
Existing approaches do not adequately model dynamic multi-scale dependencies or provide attribution-oriented interpretability.
ResDIF progressively disentangles market, sector, and individual components and uses orthogonal self-supervision for feature separation.
The authors report predictive, attributional, and portfolio-management benefits.

source_observation.claim: The framework separates hierarchical financial dynamics into market, sector, and individual layers while encouraging feature orthogonality.

interpretation.claim: Explicit structural decomposition may improve interpretability when signals arise from coupled factors at multiple levels.

application.claim: This pattern could inform forecasting systems that need both predictions and factor-level attribution.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish whether the decomposition is accurate or transferable beyond the reported experiments.
